W1700K Community Builds

Following some great discussion in the main Quantum Fiber W1700K Developer Support thread, this thread has been created as a dedicated home for community and custom builds of the W1700K.

Why this thread?

With the W1700K now officially supported in OpenWrt snapshot, the developer thread is rightly focused on upstream submissions and official builds. Custom builds — which often include experimental patches, extra drivers, performance tweaks, and other additions beyond snapshot — are a fantastic part of this community, but they belong in their own space so both streams can thrive without stepping on each other.

Community builds are where a lot of the most interesting experimentation happens.

What this thread is for

Sharing your custom W1700K builds

Helping others flash, configure, and get the most out of their device

Testing and discussing experimental patches before they go upstream

Supporting users who want more than stock snapshot offers

A big thanks to everyone in the developer thread who has put so much work into getting this device to where it is today. That foundation is what makes all of this possible.

Jump in, share your builds, and let's keep the W1700K community growing.

Caddy runs on your internal network as a reverse proxy.

You configure your FQDNs in the config and it then presents the relevant Let's Encrypt certificate for any connections on TCP 443.

This allows me to have self-signed certs and dynamic DNS, but a trusted certificate chain.

Step 1:

"Caddy Inc." connects to domain.gleeze.com on port 80 > Dynu forwards the traffic to my OpenWrt router > The router forwards it to the local server hosting Caddy > The local server downloads the required Let's Encrypt cert and stores it locally.

Step 2:

https from internet to domain.gleeze.com > openwrt router port forwards to Caddy > Caddy presents the Let's Encrypt certificate and the connection is designated as 'secure' > Caddy forwards the traffic to the relevant endpoint on the local network.

@arian-gogani thanks for the NIST pointer. The NCCoE concept paper's four pillars map onto this RFC's surface:

| NCCoE pillar | RFC surface area |
|---|---|
| Identification | signer pubkey in receipt |
| Authorization | delegation chain root / holder binding |
| Delegation | scoped authority chains with expiration |
| Logging / non-repudiation | signed receipts, hash-chained |

On @srotzin's pre-execution gap: one pattern worth capturing in the RFC is co-signing the policy decision with the action before the call is dispatched. The receipt contains the policy hash, matched rules, and decision in the same signed object as the action — so the verifier can confirm that a specific policy version produced a specific decision, without runtime access. Signet does this with PolicyAttestation; curious whether other implementers handle policy signing at call time or post-hoc.

The Q4 2026 Interoperability Profile is the normative output to watch. Multiple independent implementations converging on a shared format may strengthen the case for standardization.

Doing lots of programming over the years I've realized that I often need to write "code for myself", in my head, to think what I should do and in what order, and also why. I write to-do notes and notes on why something was best done or had to be done in a given way. Code is instructions for the computer, but developers need instructions too.It always seemed to require extra effort to "program myself", maybe because it requires questioning whether I'm doing it the right way and what would be some alternative ways of doing it. It's almost like "out-of-box thinking".Whereas basic coding is often as easy as writing this note here, just write what comes to my mind. Coding tasks are often trivial, but they must be done. But they don't really burden our mind too much, not too often.But with AI, it's all about "programming the programmer".And that requires more thinking, asking more questions like is this really what we need to accomplish, or would some alternative way be better? What alternative way?Asking questions like that was always part of the work but with AI it seems to be the only type of work. And it is more difficult, more exhausting, than basic coding.

4. Extract Kali filesystem

tar -xvf kalifs.tar.xz --strip-components=1

While on paper, blender would seem to be a marvelous program, its much less impressive in practice. Not only is it incredibly user-unfriendly (it expects users to have an encyclopedic knowledge of all of its features right out the gate to use the program), but for whatever reason, using it for more than 5ish minutes lags my whole computer, even after closing the program and trying to do other things, until I reboot the device or restart my graphics drivers. Yes, there are decades of forum posts from users and video guides online, but I shouldn't have to consult outside sources to do extremely basic things, nor should my PC start lagging from having maybe 40 polygons MAX from an unfinished model I was working on nearly brick my computer. Program could easily be a 10/10 if they sent you a damn textbook as the user manual upon downloading or automatically enrolled all of its prospective users in some semester-long course on how to use it, but as it stands, it's unfortunately more of a hassle to use than anything. Yes, its technically versatile, and I appreciate that it isn't locked behind a paywall, but nobody is gonna be able to use this program to make anything of their own unless they've sunk hours of their life reading and studying how to use the program.
